claims.text: An initially single-phase high-entropy alloy can develop brittle behavior or lose ductility at intermediate temperatures.
The brittle behavior is caused by fast, temperature-driven nanosegregation of principal alloying elements to grain boundaries.
Ni, Cr, and Mn are examples of principal elements that segregate or partition at grain boundaries in CrMnFeCoNi.
Grain-boundary segregation reduces local grain-boundary cohesion.
Reduced grain-boundary cohesion promotes crack initiation and intergranular fracture under load.
Preexisting Cr-rich grain-boundary precipitates absorb mobile embrittling principal elements.
Absorption of segregants by Cr-rich precipitates lowers segregant concentrations at active grain boundaries.
Cr-rich grain-boundary precipitates thereby mitigate grain-boundary decohesion and brittleness.
Equiatomic CrMnFeCoNi can be prepared as a single FCC solid solution by homogenization, without preexisting grain-boundary secondary phases.
An as-cast CrMnFeCoNi alloy can be assumed to have the same single-phase, precipitate-free initial state.
Annealing or heat treatment can induce Cr-rich precipitates at grain boundaries in CrMnFeCoNi.
The proposed treatment can create a controlled dual-phase microstructure with Cr-rich precipitates selectively and strategically distributed along grain boundaries.
The relevant service window is approximately 650–700°C.
The proposed mechanism applies under both tensile and creep loading.
The precipitate-engineered alloy will have a higher fracture strain than the homogenized single-phase baseline.
The precipitate-engineered alloy will exhibit ductile, dimpled rupture.
The untreated single-phase alloy will exhibit intergranular brittle cracking under the specified tests.
Segregation of minor elements to grain boundaries often embrittles conventional alloys.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis treats Cr-rich grain-boundary precipitates as beneficial sinks that improve ductility, but cited record PMC6897545::web::010::gb_segregation_engineering_to_enhance_du reports that formation of Cr-rich BCC and L10-NiMn grain-boundary phases in nanocrystalline CrMnFeCoNi substantially reduces ductility. The evidence does not demonstrate a beneficial segregant-trapping role for such precipitates.
